You are a research group coordinator who needs to document analysis of three foundational papers in language model research. Your task is to analyze three specific papers available in the paper database, create structured notes in your team's Notion workspace, and compile a formal Word report.

The three papers you need to analyze are: "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" (arXiv ID 2301.07041), "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback" (arXiv ID 2203.11171), and "OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models" (arXiv ID 2205.01068). Use the arXiv and LaTeX analysis tools to retrieve full text and analyze each paper's structure, sections, and key contributions.

For each paper, create a Notion page in your workspace with the paper title as the page title, prefixed with "Paper: ". Include structured notes in the page body covering the paper's main contributions, methodology, and key findings based on the full text you retrieve.

Create a Word document called Paper_Analysis_Report.docx in your workspace. The document should start with a title "Comparative Paper Analysis Report" and include a section for each of the three papers. Each section heading should identify the paper clearly. Within each section, describe the paper's title, key contributions, and methodology. After the three individual sections, include a final section titled "Comparative Analysis" that draws connections between the three papers, discussing how they relate to each other in terms of their contributions to large language model research.

Send an email to research_lead@university.edu with subject "Paper Analysis Report Ready" summarizing what you have done and noting that the Word document and Notion pages are ready for review.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently,

The three fixed-paper source stage is small enough for the main agent; use sub-agents only for the two independent output owners. All research is read-only.

Resolve the task-visible workspace directory from the runtime allowed-directory listing (or the literal accessible-workspace directory already supplied by the harness), freeze it as `<workspace_root>`, and reject bare `/workspace` and dumps/run-specific paths. Freeze the three task-specified ID/title slots: `2301.07041 / Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models`, `2203.11171 / Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback`, and `2205.01068 / OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models`.

Issue the arXiv record and arxiv-latex section calls for all three IDs in one native-parallel source response. Verify each returned stable ID/title even if the task's pairing is unusual; do not silently replace a task slot from outside knowledge. For each slot extract title, complete authors when returned, contributions, methodology, findings, section list/count, provenance, and missing/conflict status. Reconcile once and freeze one literal canonical three-paper packet; the Notion pages, Word report, and email consume this exact packet without re-researching or recomputing claims.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 2 coder sub-agents in parallel as individual Agent calls:

   1. coder 0 (external-workflow-operator 0): Notion owner: search exact titles `Paper: <canonical title>`; reuse one exact match, create at most one page on zero matches, and block on duplicates. Own all three pages in one agent so parent IDs and idempotency stay consistent. Each page must contain substantive Contribution, Methodology, and Findings blocks copied from the canonical packet. Read all three pages back and return IDs, exact titles, stable-ID coverage, and block validation. Do not write the Word file or email.
   2. coder 1 (office-report-builder 0): Word owner: create `<workspace_root>/Paper_Analysis_Report.docx` exactly once, preferably atomically with `python-docx`, with the required report title, one clearly headed section per canonical paper, and a final Comparative Analysis grounded only in those records. Read it back and return path, heading order, exact paper/title coverage, and validation. Do not modify Notion or email.

In the same response that launches Wave 1, the main agent paginates Sent search for exact To `research_lead@university.edu` and Subject `Paper Analysis Report Ready`, reading every candidate. After both outputs return, send exactly once only if no exact match exists, mentioning the verified Word filename and the three verified Notion page titles/IDs. Never retry an ambiguous send. Accept only after all pages, the document, and exactly one message read back against the canonical packet.

PAGE_TITLE: Paper: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models

BLOCKS (render in this exact order):
[PARAGRAPH] arXiv ID: 2301.07041 | Authors: Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan | Source: full text retrieved from the arXiv/LaTeX paper database.
[HEADING_2] Overview
[PARAGRAPH] This paper establishes empirical scaling laws for language model performance. The authors show that the cross-entropy loss decreases as a smooth power law with model size, dataset size, and the amount of compute used for training, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude. Because these relationships are predictable in advance, model performance can be forecast before training and a fixed compute budget can be allocated optimally.
[HEADING_2] Main Contributions
[BULLET] Empirically derives power-law scaling relationships between the cross-entropy loss and the three primary scaling factors: model size, dataset size, and training compute.
[BULLET] Quantifies the scaling exponents at approximately 0.076 for model parameters, 0.095 for dataset size, and 0.050 for compute.
[BULLET] Establishes that other architectural details, such as network width or depth, have minimal effect on performance within a wide range.
[BULLET] Derives simple equations governing the dependence of overfitting on model and dataset size, and the dependence of training speed on model size.
[BULLET] Provides a principled framework for predicting model performance and for optimally allocating a fixed compute budget.
[BULLET] Demonstrates that larger models are more sample-efficient.
[HEADING_2] Methodology
[PARAGRAPH] The work is an empirical scaling study rather than the proposal of a new architecture. The central analytical device is a power-law functional form fitted to observed losses. For model size, the loss L is modelled as L(N) = (N_c/N)^alpha_N, where N is the number of model parameters, N_c is a constant, and alpha_N is the scaling exponent. Analogous relationships are fitted for dataset size and for compute, with exponents of approximately 0.095 and 0.050 respectively.
[PARAGRAPH] To fit and validate these relationships the authors trained over 1,000 models spanning three orders of magnitude in scale. The fitted laws are then used analytically to determine how a fixed compute budget should be divided between training a larger model and training on more data.
[HEADING_2] Key Findings
[BULLET] The loss scales as a power law with model size, dataset size, and compute, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude.
[BULLET] The fitted exponents are approximately alpha_N = 0.076 for parameters, alpha_D = 0.095 for data, and alpha_C = 0.050 for compute.
[BULLET] Larger models trained on more data with more compute consistently achieve lower loss.
[BULLET] Architectural details such as network width or depth have minimal effect within a wide range.
[BULLET] Larger models are more sample-efficient, and the derived equations allow a fixed compute budget to be allocated optimally.
[HEADING_2] Document Structure
[BULLET] Introduction - motivates the study and states that performance scales predictably with model size, dataset size, and compute budget.
[BULLET] Scaling Laws - presents the power-law functional forms and the fitted exponents.
[BULLET] Experiments - describes the study of over 1,000 models spanning three orders of magnitude and the confirmation of the laws.
[BULLET] Conclusion - discusses implications for predicting performance and allocating compute budgets.

PAGE_TITLE: Paper: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback

BLOCKS (render in this exact order):
[PARAGRAPH] arXiv ID: 2203.11171 | Authors: Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Xu Jiang | Source: full text retrieved from the arXiv/LaTeX paper database.
[HEADING_2] Overview
[PARAGRAPH] Starting from GPT-3, this paper trains language models that are substantially better at following user instructions. The central insight is that making a language model more useful does not require ever-larger parameter counts: alignment with human intent can be achieved through a three-stage fine-tuning pipeline that combines supervised learning and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). The resulting InstructGPT models are preferred by human labelers to GPT-3 outputs, are more truthful, and are less toxic, despite having only 1.3B parameters compared to the 175B GPT-3.
[HEADING_2] Main Contributions
[BULLET] Introduces InstructGPT, a family of language models fine-tuned from GPT-3 to follow human instructions.
[BULLET] Defines and demonstrates a three-step alignment pipeline: supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, reward model training from preference comparisons, and reinforcement learning with PPO.
[BULLET] Shows that a 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT model is preferred by human evaluators to the 175B-parameter GPT-3 on 85% of prompts, a reduction of more than two orders of magnitude in parameter count.
[BULLET] Improves truthfulness on TruthfulQA and reduces toxicity relative to GPT-3.
[BULLET] Establishes that substantial alignment gains can be obtained with only minimal trade-off in general language-model capabilities.
[HEADING_2] Methodology
[PARAGRAPH] The method is a three-step pipeline applied on top of GPT-3. Step 1 is supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on human demonstration data, which teaches the model the format and style of instruction-following responses. Step 2 trains a reward model from human preference comparisons, in which labelers rank candidate outputs so that a scalar reward for response quality can be learned. Step 3 fine-tunes the language model with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), using the learned reward model as the objective.
[PARAGRAPH] Evaluation combines human preference judgments against GPT-3 outputs with standardized measurements of truthfulness on TruthfulQA and of toxicity.
[HEADING_2] Key Findings
[BULLET] InstructGPT 1.3B is preferred to GPT-3 175B by human evaluators on 85% of prompts.
[BULLET] The aligned model shows better truthfulness on TruthfulQA than GPT-3.
[BULLET] The aligned model is measurably less toxic than GPT-3.
[BULLET] RLHF achieves substantial alignment improvement with only minimal trade-off in general capabilities.
[BULLET] Alignment with user intent is therefore primarily a matter of training procedure rather than of raw scale.
[HEADING_2] Document Structure
[BULLET] Introduction - identifies the problem of unhelpful, untruthful, or toxic outputs and introduces the RLHF alignment approach.
[BULLET] Method - details the three steps: supervised fine-tuning, reward model training, and PPO fine-tuning.
[BULLET] Experiments - reports the human evaluation comparing InstructGPT 1.3B against GPT-3 175B, plus truthfulness and toxicity measurements.
[BULLET] Results - assesses the balance between alignment gains and any loss of general capability.

Comparative Analysis

Paragraph 1: These three papers address three complementary and, in combination, foundational questions in large language model research: how performance scales, how behaviour is shaped, and how access is provided.

Paragraph 2: "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" supplies the quantitative foundation on which the other two rest. By fitting power laws to loss as a function of parameters, data, and compute, it turns scale itself into a measurable and predictable quantity, and it provides the exponents needed to forecast performance and to allocate a fixed compute budget optimally. Both of the other papers implicitly depend on this kind of reasoning. OPT's decision to build a 125M-to-175B suite, and to describe the data and hardware required to reach the top of that range, is an exercise in the compute and scale planning that the scaling laws make principled. InstructGPT, meanwhile, demonstrates the limits of scale alone: its central result is that a 1.3B-parameter model preferred on 85% of prompts outperforms a 175B-parameter model at the task users actually care about, which reframes scale as only one of the variables that determine usefulness.

Paragraph 3: OPT and InstructGPT complement each other in the opposite direction. OPT attacks the access problem: before its release the only models at the 175B scale were closed, so the community could neither verify scaling predictions nor study large models directly. By releasing weights and training code, OPT makes the empirical territory that the scaling laws map out explorable rather than merely readable. InstructGPT attacks the behaviour problem: it supplies the three-step RLHF recipe, running from supervised fine-tuning through reward modelling to PPO, that converts a raw next-token predictor into a model that follows instructions. Together they suggest a division of labour in which open base models provide the substrate and alignment techniques provide usable behaviour on top of it.

Paragraph 4: A useful contrast also emerges in methodology. All three papers are empirical rather than architectural: none proposes a fundamentally new network design, and OPT deliberately uses a standard transformer with pre-norm layer normalisation, ReLU activations, and learned positional embeddings. The scaling laws paper contributes an analytical framework built on curve fitting across more than 1,000 trained models; InstructGPT contributes a training pipeline built on human preference data; OPT contributes an infrastructure and openness playbook built on 800GB of data and up to 992 A100 GPUs. Where the scaling laws ask how large a model should be, InstructGPT asks how a model should behave, and OPT asks who should be able to study one.

Paragraph 5: Read together, the papers trace a coherent arc in large language model research. The scaling laws establish the predictability of scale and the sample efficiency of larger models; OPT realises that scale in an open, reproducible form that matches GPT-3 on most benchmarks; and InstructGPT shows that alignment with human intent, achieved with a modest parameter count and minimal loss of general capability, is what converts a scaled predictor into a useful system. Each paper also constrains the others: the compute-allocation guidance of the scaling laws informs projects such as OPT, OPT's open weights enable the kind of alignment research that InstructGPT performs, and InstructGPT's demonstration that alignment can substitute for scale qualifies the pure scaling narrative.
